params.title: Receiving Systems
params.subtitle: Follow a faint echo through the radar receiver: mixer, local oscillator and AFC, IF and video amplifiers, clutter, noise and power.

onScreen: Follow an echo from the antenna to the display
scenes.narration: Welcome to Receiving Systems. A radar receiver has one big job: take an echo so faint it's barely there and turn it into a clear spot on the screen. We'll follow that echo from the antenna to the display. Along the way you'll meet the circuit that keeps the receiver tuned, the controls that clean up echoes from the waves, the noise that hides small targets, and the power supplies behind it all. When a radar picture goes blank, fuzzy or cluttered, a technician who understands these stages knows where to look. You need no electronics background: we'll build from the basics, and by the end you'll be able to trace an echo through the receiver and answer every exam question on it.

params.title: How a radar sees
labels: The magnetron sends out a short, powerful burst of microwaves: a pulse
A target returns a tiny echo, like a shout echoing off a cliff
The echo's delay gives range; the antenna's direction gives bearing
Each echo becomes a spot on the display

onScreen: Short microwave pulse from the magnetron
Delay gives range, direction gives bearing
scenes.narration: Let's start with how radar works. The heart of the transmitter is the magnetron, a special vacuum tube: a sealed container with the air pumped out. It fires a very short, powerful burst of microwaves, the same kind of energy a microwave oven uses. That burst is called a pulse, and it goes out from a turning antenna. When the pulse hits a ship or a coastline, a tiny part of it bounces back, like a shout echoing off a cliff. The longer the echo takes to return, the farther away the target is: that distance is its range. The direction the antenna is pointing gives the target's bearing. Each echo becomes a spot on the display, at its range and bearing.

params.title: One antenna, and a very weak echo
items: The same antenna sends the pulse and hears the echo
The duplexer switches it: to the transmitter during each pulse, to the receiver after
The echo that returns is fantastically weak: a few millionths of a volt
The receiver's job: turn that whisper into a bright spot

onScreen: The receiver turns it into a bright spot
scenes.narration: The same antenna both sends and listens, so something has to switch it. That's the duplexer: it connects the antenna to the transmitter during each pulse, and to the receiver the rest of the time. Now think about what comes back. The pulse leaves with enormous power, but only a sliver of it hits the target, and only a sliver of that returns. So the echo is fantastically weak, often just a few millionths of a volt. A volt is the unit of electrical push, the pressure that drives electricity through a circuit. The receiver's job is to turn that whisper into a bright spot on the display.

onScreen: A radar receiver is a microwave receiver
scenes.narration: What kind of signal is that echo? Every radio wave vibrates back and forth, and the number of vibrations each second is its frequency, measured in hertz. A megahertz is a million vibrations a second. Shortwave radio, called HF for high frequency, works at 3 to 30 megahertz. FM broadcast radio, FM for frequency modulation, sits around 100 megahertz. Radar goes far higher, into microwaves, counted in gigahertz: a gigahertz is 1000 megahertz. Ship radars use S-band, near 3 gigahertz, or X-band, near 9.4 gigahertz. So when the exam asks what radar receivers are similar to, the answer is microwave receivers. Not FM, HF or television receivers: they all work at far lower frequencies.

params.title: Why the receiver changes the echo's frequency
items: Microwaves are awkward: ordinary wires waste them, so radar uses waveguide
Amplifiers that work directly at microwave frequencies were hard to build
So the receiver first converts the echo to a much lower frequency
That's the RF mixer: it converts a low-level signal to a different frequency

onScreen: Microwave amplifiers were hard to build
Convert the echo to a lower frequency
RF mixer: converts a low-level signal to a different frequency
scenes.narration: So the echo is a weak microwave signal, and microwaves are awkward to handle. In ordinary wires, much of their energy is wasted, so radar carries them in waveguide: hollow metal tubing that channels microwaves the way a pipe channels water. Making them stronger takes an amplifier, a circuit that makes a signal bigger, and microwave amplifiers were hard to build. So the classic radar receiver doesn't try: it first converts the echo to a much lower frequency, where amplifying is easy. That's the job of the RF, or radio frequency, mixer. On the exam, an RF mixer converts a low-level signal, meaning a weak one, to a different frequency. It doesn't form the transmitted pulses or add audio tones.

blocks.label: Local oscillator
blocks.note: A steady signal, made in the receiver

blocks.label: IF: the difference
blocks.note: Typically 30 or 60 MHz, easy to amplify

onScreen: The echo, a weak microwave signal
The difference: the IF, typically 30 or 60 MHz
scenes.narration: How does the mixer change the frequency? It combines the echo with a second, steady signal from the local oscillator. An oscillator is a circuit that generates a steady wave, and local means it's right here in the receiver. When 2 frequencies are mixed, a new one appears at their difference, a bit like 2 slightly out-of-tune guitar strings making a slow wobble. That difference is called the intermediate frequency, or IF: intermediate because it sits between the microwave echo and the final picture signal. A radar's IF is typically 30 or 60 megahertz, low enough to amplify easily.

blocks.label: Crystal mixer
blocks.note: Converts the echo down to the IF

onScreen: Duplexer straight to the crystal mixer
Video amplifier sends signals to the display
scenes.narration: Here's the whole receiver chain, in the order the echo travels. The echo leaves the duplexer and goes straight to the crystal mixer, which converts it down to the IF. The IF amplifier boosts it. Next, the second detector strips away the IF and keeps just the shape of each echo pulse. That pulse signal is called video, because it's what draws the picture. Notice the crossed-out box: there's no RF amplifier ahead of the mixer. The local oscillator feeds the mixer. And the display gets its signals from the video amplifier, the section of the receiving system that sends signals to the display system. The IF amplifier feeds the detector, not the display, and there's no audio stage, because there's no sound.

params.title: Where the gain comes from
rows: The echo goes straight to the mixer
Converting the echo costs some strength
Easy to amplify at the IF

onScreen: IF amplifier: nearly all the gain
scenes.narration: Now that crossed-out box. Gain is how many times bigger an amplifier makes a signal. So where does a radar receiver get its gain? Not at the front end, the part the echo meets first: the front end does not provide any amplification to the radar signal. There's no RF amplifier at all, so a radar receiver's RF power amplifier does not exist. The crystal mixer doesn't help either: it has a conversion loss, so a little less signal comes out than goes in. Nearly all the amplification happens after conversion, in the IF amplifier. One more trap: the IF amplifier is not always narrow, passing only a thin slice of frequencies. How wide it is changes with the range shown, as we'll see.

params.title: The TR cell guards the mixer

blocks.label: Duplexer
blocks.note: Shared by the pulse and the echoes

blocks.label: TR cell
blocks.note: A gas-filled tube guarding the mixer

scenes.narration: With no amplifier in front of it, the crystal mixer is the first thing the echo meets, and that crystal is delicate. Follow the paths. The magnetron's pulse goes through the duplexer and out to the antenna. The echoes come back the same way and turn off toward the mixer. So what stops the pulse from turning toward the mixer too? Its power is enormous, and it would burn the crystal out in an instant. The guard is an ion discharge TR, or transmit-receive, cell: a small gas-filled tube in the receiver's path, inside the duplexer.

params.title: The TR cell protects the mixer
rows: Ionizes and shorts the receiver path

onScreen: During the pulse: the TR cell ionizes and shorts the receiver path
After the pulse: it deionizes and passes the echoes
scenes.narration: Here's how the TR cell works. During the transmit pulse, the strong energy ionizes the gas: electrons, the tiny charged particles in every atom, are knocked loose, so the gas conducts, letting electricity flow through it, much like a neon sign lighting up. That short-circuits the receiver path, so the pulse is turned away before it reaches the mixer. After the pulse, the gas deionizes and stops conducting, and the weak echoes pass through. So a TR cell is used to protect the receiver mixer during the transmit pulse. It doesn't protect the transmitter, lower the noise or tune anything.

params.title: A diode is nonlinear
items: Current: the flow of electrons through a circuit
A diode lets current through one way only, like a one-way valve
Nonlinear: its current doesn't rise in step with the voltage
Feed it 2 frequencies, and their difference appears

scenes.narration: So the TR cell guards the mixer. Now let's look inside the mixer itself. What actually does the mixing? A diode. First, current is the flow of electrons through a circuit. A diode is a part that lets current pass one way but not the other, like a one-way valve in a water pipe. The key is that a diode is nonlinear: its current doesn't rise in step with the voltage. A small push gives almost nothing, and a little more gives a lot. Feed it the echo and the local oscillator signal together, and that uneven response distorts their combined wave. The distortion contains new frequencies, including the difference between the two. That's mixing.

params.title: The crystal diode does the conversion
items: In the receive mode, a crystal diode does the frequency conversion
Traditionally a tiny silicon crystal touched by a fine wire
Not a pentagrid converter: it can't work at microwave frequencies
Not waveguide sections or ferrite devices: they don't mix signals

onScreen: Silicon crystal and a fine wire
scenes.narration: In the receive mode, then, frequency conversion is generally done by a crystal diode. Its name comes from its makeup: traditionally a tiny piece of silicon crystal touched by a fine wire. Silicon is a semiconductor, a material whose ability to carry current can be controlled, which is what makes this kind of diode possible. The exam's other choices fail. A pentagrid converter is a vacuum tube named for its 5 grids, wire screens inside it. It mixed signals in old broadcast radios, but it can't work at microwave frequencies. Tunable waveguide sections only carry microwaves, and ferrite devices, magnetic parts, only steer them. Neither one mixes signals.

params.title: For the exam: what the mixer uses
rows: Choose it: a semiconductor diode device
A tube or a transistor stage
Only PIN diodes, or only silicon crystals

onScreen: For the exam: silicon crystal or PIN diode
Not a tube or transistor stage
For the exam: PIN diodes and silicon crystals
In practice, PIN diodes protect and switch receivers
scenes.narration: The exam asks what the mixer uses in 2 more questions, and both keyed answers are questionable. First, for the exam, the radar mixer uses a silicon crystal or PIN diode. A PIN diode is a diode with 3 layers: P-type and N-type silicon, treated to carry current in different ways, with pure, or intrinsic, silicon between them. Either way, it's a semiconductor diode device, not a vacuum tube or a transistor, the part that amplifies in most electronics. The second question lists the types separately. For the exam, the mixer uses PIN diodes and silicon crystals together; an answer naming only one is incomplete. In practice, PIN diodes mostly protect and switch receivers rather than mix, but these are the answers the exam expects.

callouts.label: RF echoes at 4095 MHz come in at the top
Local oscillator: 4155 MHz CW, a steady continuous wave
They meet at the crystal diode
The tuned transformer passes the difference: 4155 − 4095 = 60 MHz

scenes.narration: Now let's see a mixer circuit: the exam's Figure 8C9. RF echoes at 4095 megahertz come in at the top. The local oscillator's signal comes in below, at 4155 megahertz. It's marked CW, continuous wave, meaning a steady, unbroken signal. Both meet at the crystal diode, which mixes them. On the right is a tuned transformer: 2 coils sharing a magnetic field, tuned so they pass only one frequency, here 60 megahertz. Why 60? It's the difference: 4155 minus 4095 is 60 megahertz. So the local oscillator sits exactly one IF above the echoes, and every echo comes out as a 60 megahertz burst, ready for the IF amplifier.

callouts.label: No echoes: only the 4155 MHz local oscillator reaches the diode
The diode just rectifies it to steady DC
No 60 MHz difference to pass: no output is developed

onScreen: No echoes: only the local oscillator reaches the diode
The diode rectifies it to DC
scenes.narration: Here's the exam's question: what does the circuit in Figure 8C9 put out when no echoes are being received? Take the echoes away, and only the steady local oscillator reaches the diode. With nothing to mix it with, the diode simply rectifies it. Rectifying means letting the current through in one direction only, which turns the back-and-forth signal into DC, direct current, flowing one way. There's no difference frequency, so nothing at 60 megahertz exists for the tuned transformer to pass. The answer: no output is developed. The trap answers name 60, 4095 or 4155 megahertz CW. The echoes and their 60 megahertz difference simply aren't there, and the tuned transformer won't pass the 4155 megahertz local oscillator.

params.title: What the local oscillator must do
items: Make a steady, low-power microwave signal
Sit exactly one IF away from the echoes
Tune easily, so it can follow the transmitter
In a radar unit, the local oscillator is a klystron

onScreen: One IF away from the echoes
In a radar unit: a klystron
scenes.narration: That's the mixer. Its partner, the local oscillator, has so far just been a box that feeds it. What does it need to do? First, make a steady, low-power microwave signal. It only has to drive a diode, so a small signal is plenty. Second, sit exactly one IF away from the echoes, like 4155 megahertz against echoes at 4095. Third, be easy to tune, because the transmitter's frequency wanders a little, and the local oscillator has to follow it. In a radar unit, the device that does all this is a klystron. Let's see how it works.

blocks.label: Hot cathode
blocks.note: Shoots out a stream of electrons

blocks.label: Resonant cavity
blocks.note: A metal chamber that rings at one frequency

onScreen: Resonant cavity rings at one frequency
scenes.narration: A reflex klystron is another small vacuum tube. With the air pumped out, electrons can fly freely inside. At one end, a hot cathode, a heated metal part, boils off a stream of electrons. They fly through a resonant cavity: a hollow metal chamber that rings at one frequency, the way a bottle hums one note when you blow across it. Beyond the cavity sits the repeller, also called the reflector. Electrons are negative, and like charges repel, so the negative repeller turns them around and sends them back through the cavity. Reflex means reflected. Out of the cavity comes low-power microwave energy.

params.title: How the klystron keeps ringing
items: Passing the cavity, some electrons are sped up and others slowed
Turned back by the repeller, they return in bunches
Each bunch pushes the cavity in time with its ringing, like pushes on a swing
The repeller voltage sets the timing, so the klystron tunes electronically

onScreen: Some electrons sped up, others slowed
Each bunch pushes the cavity in time
scenes.narration: But how does it keep ringing? As the electrons pass through the cavity, its ringing speeds some of them up and slows others down. Out at the repeller, the fast ones travel farther before they're turned back, and the slow ones turn back sooner, so they return together in bunches. Each bunch arrives just in time to give the cavity a push, like pushing a swing at the right moment, and that keeps the ringing going. The timing depends on the repeller voltage. Change that voltage, and the bunches arrive a little earlier or later. That's why a klystron can be tuned electronically.

params.title: The local oscillator: klystron or Gunn diode
rows: Semiconductor slab that oscillates on DC

onScreen: Answer: a klystron and a Gunn diode
scenes.narration: The klystron isn't the only choice. Newer radars are solid-state, meaning built from semiconductors, with no vacuum tubes. Their local oscillator is often a Gunn diode: a tiny slab of semiconductor that oscillates at microwave frequencies when DC is applied. So when the exam asks what devices could be used as the local oscillator in a radar receiver, choose both, a klystron and a Gunn diode: the reflex klystron in older sets, the Gunn diode oscillator in solid-state sets. An answer naming only one is incomplete. But when it asks what the local oscillator in a radar unit is, the answer is simply a klystron. Don't pick the hydrogen thyratron: it's a fast switching tube in the modulator, the circuit that fires the magnetron.

onScreen: It changes the electrons' transit time
Not anode voltage or buncher grids
Large changes: size of the resonant cavity
scenes.narration: Back to the klystron, and how it's tuned. How is its frequency varied? 2 ways, one fine and one coarse. Small changes are made by adjusting the repeller voltage. That changes the electrons' transit time, how long they take to turn around and come back, and the cavity's ringing shifts slightly to stay in step with the bunches. Not the anode voltage, and not the phasing of buncher grids: those are trap answers. Large changes are made by adjusting the size of the resonant cavity, mechanically. A bigger chamber rings at a lower frequency, like a bigger bottle. A choice that just says adjust the frequency explains nothing. Remember: repeller voltage for small changes, cavity size for large ones.

params.title: Why the receiver needs AFC
items: The magnetron's frequency drifts as it warms up and ages
The IF amplifier stays tuned to one frequency, such as 60 MHz
If the difference moves, the echoes slide out of the IF window
AFC, automatic frequency control, retunes the klystron to follow

onScreen: The IF amplifier stays on one frequency
Echoes slide out of the IF window
scenes.narration: So a klystron can be tuned. But why must it follow the transmitter at all? The magnetron isn't perfectly steady: its frequency drifts as it warms up and as it ages. Meanwhile the IF amplifier stays tuned to one frequency, say 60 megahertz. If the magnetron moves and the local oscillator doesn't, the difference moves too, and the echoes slide out of the IF amplifier's window, like a radio drifting off its station. A magnetron can't practically be retuned while it's running. So instead, a circuit called AFC, automatic frequency control, retunes the klystron to keep the difference steady.

onScreen: Not the receiver gain or the incoming pulses
scenes.narration: So on the exam, the AFC system is used to control the frequency of the klystron, not the magnetron. It keeps the receiver tuned to the transmitted signal by varying the frequency of the local oscillator, holding it one IF away from the magnetron. The magnetron is simply left to drift. AFC doesn't control the receiver gain, and it can't change the frequency of the incoming pulses: they come back on whatever frequency the magnetron sent. Nor does it retune the IF amplifier stage or the cavity duplexer. It moves the local oscillator, and only that.

params.title: Klystron and magnetron: one IF apart

scenes.narration: Let's put numbers on it, with an exam example. In the formula, f stands for frequency. A radar transmitter, the magnetron, is operating on 3.0 gigahertz. Its reflex klystron local oscillator runs at 3.060 gigahertz, a little above. The echoes come back on the magnetron's frequency, so the IF is the difference: the klystron frequency minus the magnetron frequency. 3.060 gigahertz minus 3.000 gigahertz leaves 60 thousandths of a gigahertz. Since a gigahertz is 1000 megahertz, that's 60 megahertz, a standard radar IF. Does it make sense? Yes: the local oscillator sits one IF above the transmitter, just as it sat one IF above the echoes in Figure 8C9.

callouts.label: Top row: the echo path, from the waveguide to the display
Crystal detector here means the main mixer
Then the IF amplifier, detector and video amplifier, to the CRT display
Block 48, between the rows, feeds both rows
Bottom row: the AFC loop, starting from the magnetron
The loop's output runs back up to block 48

onScreen: IF amplifier, detector, video amplifier, CRT
scenes.narration: So how does AFC actually do it? The exam answers with a block diagram, Figure 8A1, so let's find our way around it. Along the top runs the echo path you know: echoes arrive from the waveguide, pass the first box and reach a block labeled crystal detector, which here means the main mixer. Then come the IF amplifier, the detector, meaning our second detector, and the video amplifier, which drives the CRT, a cathode ray tube display. Block 48, between the rows, feeds both rows. The bottom row is the AFC loop. It starts with a sample from the magnetron and passes through blocks 47, 49 and 50 to an output circuit, whose line runs back up to block 48. Next, we'll name each numbered block.

blocks.label: Block 47: RF attenuator
blocks.note: Cuts the sample to a safe level

onScreen: Between the magnetron and the AFC section
scenes.narration: The AFC loop starts by taking a small sample of the magnetron's output. Even a small sample of such a powerful pulse would overload the delicate crystal that comes next. So it first passes through an RF attenuator: a part that deliberately weakens a signal by a set amount, like sunglasses for the crystal. When the exam asks where an RF attenuator is used in a radar unit, the answer is between the magnetron and the AFC section of the receiver. Not between the antenna and the receiver, where it would weaken the precious echoes, or between the magnetron and the antenna, where it would waste the transmitter's power. In Figure 8A1, it's block 47, guarding the crystal in block 49.

blocks.label: Block 49: crystal detector
blocks.note: The mixer of the AFC section

onScreen: Block 49: crystal detector, the AFC mixer
On to the AFC IF amplifier
scenes.narration: The weakened magnetron sample goes on to block 49. When the exam asks what block 49 is, the answer is the crystal detector, the mixer. It's a crystal diode, just like the main mixer, serving the AFC section. It isn't the discriminator, the IF amplifier, or the klystron. The klystron is its other input, arriving from block 48. The main mixer takes the difference between the klystron and the echoes; this one takes the difference between the klystron and the magnetron. Since the echoes come back on the magnetron's frequency, that difference, called the AFC IF, should equal the IF, about 60 megahertz. It goes on to the AFC IF amplifier.

onScreen: Block 50: discriminator, between the AFC IF amplifier and the output circuit
Too high or too low: DC of one polarity or the other
scenes.narration: After the AFC IF amplifier comes block 50, the discriminator, which feeds the AFC output circuit. It turns a frequency error into a voltage, like a tuning meter whose needle sits in the center when a station is tuned exactly. If the AFC IF is right on its center frequency, out comes 0 volts: no correction. Too high, and out comes DC of one polarity, positive say. Too low, and it's the other polarity, negative. That sign tells the loop which way to steer the klystron. And the farther off it is, the bigger the voltage, so a big error gets a big correction. So the discriminator is the circuit that develops the AFC voltage, not the peak detector, crystal mixer or second detector.

params.title: What the discriminator is for
items: It compares the frequencies of the magnetron and klystron
It generates a corrective voltage for controlling the klystron's frequency
It does not discriminate against nearby objects or similar bearings
In a radar set, it does not demodulate an FM signal

onScreen: Corrective voltage for the klystron local oscillator
Not for nearby objects or similar bearings
scenes.narration: The exam asks about the discriminator 2 more ways. In the AFC system, the discriminator compares the frequencies of the magnetron and the klystron, checking whether their difference equals the nominal, or intended, IF. And the purpose of the discriminator circuit in a radar set is to generate a corrective voltage for controlling the frequency of the klystron local oscillator. Watch the tempting wrong answers. To discriminate means to tell things apart, so 2 choices claim it discriminates against nearby objects, or against 2 objects with very similar bearings. Not so. And in an FM broadcast radio, a discriminator does demodulate, pulling the sound out of the FM signal. But not in a radar set.

onScreen: Correction voltage goes to the repeller
scenes.narration: That correction voltage, also called the error voltage, is amplified by the AFC output circuit and sent up to block 48. Block 48 is the klystron, the local oscillator. It feeds both the main crystal detector, which mixes the echoes, and block 49, the AFC mixer, and it receives the correction voltage from the AFC output circuit. Inside the klystron, the error voltage from the discriminator is applied to the repeller, also called the reflector, because changing the repeller voltage shifts the klystron's frequency electronically. It doesn't go to the magnetron, or to the IF or RF amplifiers.

onScreen: Magnetron drifts higher: the IF shrinks
scenes.narration: Back to our numbers. The magnetron transmits at 3.0 gigahertz. The klystron sits at 3.060 gigahertz, 60 megahertz above it, and that difference is the IF, right where the IF amplifier is tuned. Now suppose the magnetron drifts higher, as it does when it warms up. The gap between them shrinks, so the IF shrinks below 60 megahertz. To restore the gap, the klystron must move higher too. So should the AFC system make the klystron repeller plate more positive, more negative, less positive or less negative? More negative. A more negative repeller pushes back harder on the electrons, so they return sooner. The bunches arrive sooner, the cavity's ringing quickens to keep step, and the klystron's frequency rises. The IF is back to 60 megahertz.

params.title: Figure 8A1: once around the AFC loop

callouts.label: 47: the RF attenuator weakens a magnetron sample
49: the AFC mixer mixes it with the klystron signal
The AFC IF amplifier boosts their difference
50: the discriminator turns any error into a voltage
The output circuit sends it to the repeller of 48, the klystron
The klystron is kept on frequency automatically

scenes.narration: Let's go once around the loop. Block 47, the RF attenuator, weakens a sample of the magnetron's pulse. Block 49, the AFC mixer, mixes it with the klystron's signal, and the AFC IF amplifier boosts their difference. Block 50, the discriminator, turns any error in that difference into a voltage. The output circuit sends the voltage to the repeller of block 48, the klystron, which moves back on frequency. No one touches a knob. So the klystron local oscillator is constantly kept on frequency by the automatic frequency control circuit, which follows the drift whether the magnetron or the klystron itself wanders. Not by constant manual adjustments, or a feedback loop from the crystal detector or the TR box, which is the TR cell.

params.title: Bandwidth: how wide a window
items: Bandwidth: the range of frequencies a circuit lets through
A short, sharp pulse is made of a wide spread of frequencies
The shorter the pulse, the wider the bandwidth it needs
Radar pulses need a bandwidth of several megahertz

onScreen: Bandwidth: the range of frequencies passed
Sharp pulses: a wide spread of frequencies
scenes.narration: With the receiver held in tune, let's follow the echo into the IF amplifier. First, an idea we'll need: bandwidth. Bandwidth is the range of frequencies a circuit lets through, like the number of lanes on a highway. A smooth, steady tone fits in a single narrow lane. But a short pulse, with sudden on and off edges, is really built from a wide spread of frequencies. The shorter and sharper the pulse, the wider that spread. Squeeze it through too narrow a window and the sharp edges get rounded off, smearing the pulse. Radar pulses can last less than a millionth of a second, so they need a bandwidth of several megahertz.

So which IF do radars use? The usual IF of a shipboard radar unit is 30 or 60 megahertz. Why so high? The IF signal has to carry the full several-megahertz bandwidth of the pulses, and that only fits comfortably on a frequency many times higher. You may notice that Figure 8A1 prints 30 or 40 megahertz on its IF amplifier, but for the exam question on the usual IF, the answer is 30 or 60 megahertz. Don't confuse it with 455 kilohertz or 10.7 megahertz. Those are the IFs of AM, amplitude modulation, and FM broadcast receivers, which only need room for voice and music.

params.title: Pulse length follows the range scale
items: The range scale: how far out the picture reaches, chosen by the operator
Short ranges: short pulses, so close targets' echoes don't run together
Long ranges: longer pulses, putting more energy onto distant targets

onScreen: Range scale: how far out the picture reaches
scenes.narration: Remember the early trap, that the IF amplifier isn't always narrow? Here's why. First, what does the radar send? The operator picks a range scale: how far out the picture reaches, from a short range close around the ship to a long one far out. On short ranges, the radar sends short pulses. A short pulse lets it separate targets that are close together, because their echoes don't run into each other. On long ranges, it sends longer pulses. They put more energy onto distant targets, so their faint echoes come back stronger.

params.title: IF bandwidth switches with range
rows: Less noise for weak distant echoes

onScreen: Short range: short pulse, wide IF bandwidth
Long range: long pulse, narrow IF bandwidth
Narrow bandwidth lets in less noise
scenes.narration: So the IF bandwidth follows the pulse length. Short pulses need a wide bandwidth to keep their sharp edges; longer pulses need less. And there's a bonus. Noise, the random electrical hiss present in every receiver, is spread across all frequencies, so a narrower window lets in less of it. That helps weak, distant echoes stand out. On the exam, then, the IF amplifier bandwidth is wide for short ranges and narrow for long ranges. The wrong choices have it backward, call it constant for all ranges, or say it's adjustable from the control panel. It switches automatically with the range in use.

onScreen: Gain in dB = 20 × log of the voltage ratio
scenes.narration: How much gain does the IF amplifier give? Radar gains are so large that we count them in decibels. Here's the idea. The log, short for logarithm, of a number tells you how many 10s you multiply together to get it. The log of 10 is 1, the log of 100 is 2, and the log of 1000 is 3. For voltage, gain in decibels is 20 times the log of the voltage ratio: the output voltage divided by the input voltage. So an amplifier that makes the voltage 10 times bigger has a gain of 20 decibels, 100 times is 40 decibels, and 1000 times is 60 decibels. Each extra 20 decibels means another 10 times bigger.

The exam's version: high-gain IF amplifiers may take a 2 microvolt input up to a 2 volt output. What's the gain? A microvolt is a millionth of a volt. The formula: G, the gain, equals 20 log of V sub out over V sub in, the output and input voltages. Step 1, divide: 2 volts over 2 microvolts is a million, which is 10 to the 6th power, a 1 followed by 6 zeros. Step 2, the log of 10 to the 6th is 6. Step 3, 20 times 6 is 120. So the gain is 120 decibels. Does that make sense? Each 20 decibels is another 10 times, and 6 steps of 10 make a million. The other choices, 60, 100 and 1000 decibels, don't fit.

params.title: Every amplifier has a ceiling
items: Every amplifier has a ceiling: an output it can't go above
Push past it and the signal's tops are clipped: the amplifier is saturated
Echoes range from faint to thousands of times stronger

scenes.narration: All that gain brings a problem. Every amplifier has a ceiling, an output it can't go above. Push it harder and the tops of the signal are flattened, or clipped, and the amplifier is said to be saturated. Anything bigger than the ceiling comes out the same size. And radar echoes vary enormously: a big ship close by can be thousands of times stronger than a distant buoy. So how should a receiver handle such a spread?

params.title: Linear or logarithmic receiver
rows: Rises with the log of the input

scenes.narration: There are 2 ways to answer. In a linear receiver, the output follows the input in step: double in means double out. A very strong echo then slams into the ceiling and clips, and 2 strong echoes can look the same. A logarithmic receiver's output rises with the logarithm of the input instead: each 10 times more input adds just one more equal step of output. That's why logarithmic receivers can't be saturated: even very strong echoes still give distinct, unclipped responses. That suits radar well, so don't pick the choice saying they shouldn't be used in radar. And can't be saturated doesn't mean can't be damaged, nor do they have low sensitivity.

params.title: Why a logarithmic IF amplifier
items: Dynamic range: the span from the weakest to the strongest signal handled
A logarithmic IF amplifier has a greater dynamic range, without saturating
Not higher gain, easier alignment or a lower noise figure

onScreen: Dynamic range: weakest to strongest signal
Not higher gain or lower noise figure
scenes.narration: The same idea applies to the IF amplifier. The span from the weakest signal an amplifier can use to the strongest it can handle without saturating is called its dynamic range. A logarithmic IF amplifier is preferable to a linear one in a radar receiver because it has a greater dynamic range. It handles very weak and very strong echoes alike. The trap answers claim it has higher gain, is more easily aligned, meaning tuned up, or has a lower noise figure, a measure of how much noise an amplifier adds. None of those is inherently better in a logarithmic amplifier. Its advantage is dynamic range, not gain.

params.title: AGC and IAGC: 20 to 40 dB
items: AGC, automatic gain control: turns the gain down for strong signals
IAGC, instantaneous AGC: does it fast, echo by echo
In a radar receiver, they can vary between 20 and 40 dB
Keeps strong echoes and clutter from saturating the IF strip

onScreen: AGC: gain down for strong signals
Keeps the IF strip from saturating
scenes.narration: Another way to stop saturation is to turn the gain down when signals are strong. That's AGC, automatic gain control: a circuit that lowers the gain when the signal is strong, the way you squint in bright sunlight. IAGC, instantaneous automatic gain control, does the same thing very quickly, fast enough to act on individual echoes. In a radar receiver, AGC and IAGC can vary between 20 and 40 decibels. From our decibel table, that's a voltage change of 10 to 100 times. It's enough to keep strong echoes and clutter, the unwanted echoes from waves and rain, from saturating the IF strip, the chain of IF amplifier stages, while weak echoes keep full gain.

params.title: For the exam: overcoupling causes oscillations
items: The IF strip: several tuned stages coupled together
Coupling: how much energy passes from one stage to the next
For the exam: overcoupling causes oscillations
In practice, overcoupling mainly broadens the response

onScreen: IF strip: tuned stages coupled together
Coupling: energy passed stage to stage
For the exam: overcoupling causes oscillations
scenes.narration: One more IF question. Each stage in the IF strip is tuned to the IF and hands its signal to the next through a coupling, often a small transformer. Coupling is how much energy passes between stages; overcoupling means too much. This question is flagged: its keyed answer is doubtful. For the exam, overcoupling in a radar receiver causes oscillations. The reasoning: with so much gain, excess coupling feeds energy back from output to input, and the strip starts making a signal of its own, like a microphone howling near its speaker. In practice, overcoupling mainly widens the band of frequencies passed, but oscillations is the answer the exam expects. It doesn't improve target returns, increase the IAGC range or decrease noise.

params.title: From the IF amplifier to the display

onScreen: Video amplifier: between the IF amplifier and the display
scenes.narration: That's the IF amplifier, but a boosted echo still isn't a picture. Each echo is a short burst of IF waves, at 30 or 60 megahertz. The second detector takes that burst and keeps only its outline: a simple pulse, the video, that's on while the echo lasts. The video amplifier then boosts it to drive the display. So the full path runs mixer, IF amplifier, second detector, video amplifier, display, and the video amplifier is located between the IF amplifier and the display system. Wrong choices place it between the mixer and the IF amplifier, or between the local oscillator and the mixer. And it handles the detected pulses, not signals of 60 to 120 megahertz, which belong back on the IF side.

params.title: The second detector: a diode
labels: Each echo is a burst of IF energy: amplitude modulated
A diode detector keeps the outline, called the envelope
That outline is the video pulse
Discriminators and ratio detectors are FM detectors

onScreen: A diode detector keeps the envelope
The envelope is the video pulse
Not a discriminator or ratio detector
scenes.narration: Why is it called the second detector? The mixer counts as the first detector; the exam's question on Figure 8C9 calls it exactly that. So which kind of circuit is this second one? Each echo is a burst of IF energy whose strength, or amplitude, rises and falls with the echo: an amplitude-modulated signal, like AM radio. A detector for that simply rectifies it with a diode, then smooths it, leaving just the outline, called the envelope. So the video, or second, detector in a pulse radar most likely uses a diode detector. The other choices, the discriminator and the ratio detector, are FM detectors. They respond to changes in frequency, not strength, so they'd miss the echo pulses.

params.title: Video amplifiers need a broad bandwidth
labels: Detected echo pulses are weak and very short
A broad-bandwidth amplifier boosts them and keeps their sharp edges
A narrow amplifier would smear and shrink them

onScreen: Narrow bandwidth smears and shrinks them
scenes.narration: Next, the video amplifier itself. Why must video amplifiers in pulse radar receivers have a broad bandwidth? The exam's answer: because weak pulses must be amplified. Fresh from the detector, the echo pulses are both weak and very short. Remember bandwidth: a short pulse with sharp edges is made of a wide spread of frequencies. A broad-bandwidth amplifier boosts all of them, so the pulses come out big and still sharp. A narrow amplifier would smear and shrink them, and a small target's pulse could fade away. The other choices mention high frequency sine waves, or pulses that are too wide. The video amplifier handles pulses, and they're narrow, not wide.

params.title: What rounds off a pulse
items: Capacitor: a part that stores electric charge
Every stage's input, output and wiring acts like a small capacitor
It must fill or empty before the voltage can change: corners round off
The cure: an inductor, a coil that keeps current moving

scenes.narration: What threatens those sharp edges? Capacitance. A capacitor is a part that stores electric charge, and every amplifier stage's input and output, and even the wiring, acts like a small one. Before the voltage can change, that capacitance has to fill or empty, which rounds off the corners of each pulse, like a sponge soaking up the first rush of water. The cure is a coil of wire, called an inductor. An inductor resists changes in current, so once current is flowing it keeps it moving, which helps charge that capacitance faster.

params.title: Peaking coils keep video pulses sharp

onScreen: Series: one after the other; parallel: side by side
Inductor in series with the input capacitance
Inductor in parallel with the output capacitance
scenes.narration: Where do the coils go? First, 2 words you'll need. In series means one after the other, in the same path, like links in a chain. In parallel means side by side, across each other, like 2 lanes of a road. In video amplifiers, an inductor is connected in series with the input capacitance, called series peaking, and an inductor in parallel with the output capacitance, called shunt peaking; shunt is another word for parallel. Remember: series at the input, parallel at the output. The traps swap them, put coils in parallel with both, or use resistors, which don't keep current moving.

blocks.label: Sweep and deflection circuits
blocks.note: Turn the trace with the antenna

onScreen: Range markers: a video amplifier input
scenes.narration: What else goes into the video amplifier besides the echoes? The exam asks both ways. Range markers are usual inputs: they're the electronic rings drawn on the screen at set distances, mixed right into the video. So are the brilliance and contrast settings, the operator's brightness and contrast controls, which set the level of the video sent to the display. So which are usual inputs? All of them: range, brilliance and contrast. But the resolver is not usually an input to the video amplifier. A resolver is a sensor at the antenna that reports which way it's pointing. It carries that bearing information to the sweep and deflection circuits, which swing the trace, the line that paints the picture, around in step with the antenna.

params.title: Sea return
labels: Sea return: reflections of radar signals from nearby waves
Clutter around the center of the display
Strongest at short range and in rough seas
A small boat close by can vanish inside it

onScreen: Sea return: reflections from nearby waves
Strongest at short range and in rough seas
scenes.narration: Now the picture is on the screen, along with things you don't want to see. The first is sea return, also called sea clutter. Sea return is the reflection of radar signals from nearby waves. Every wave face near the ship acts like a tiny target. On the PPI, or plan position indicator, the map-like display with your ship at the center, it shows up as speckle all around your ship. It's strongest at short range, where the waves are hit by the strongest energy, and in rough seas, where the waves are bigger and steeper. A small boat close by can vanish inside it. The trap answers call sea return sea water in the antenna, or the echo from a target at sea.

onScreen: Close objects: gain cut right after each pulse
Acts on the receiver, not the transmitter
scenes.narration: The fix is a circuit called STC, sensitivity time control. Sensitivity is how weak an echo the receiver can pick up, set by its gain. STC decreases the sensitivity of the receiver for close objects. Right after each pulse goes out, it cuts the receiver gain, then lets it rise with time. Why does that work? Echoes from close objects, including the waves, come back first, and they meet low gain. Echoes from distant objects arrive later, when the gain is back to full. It's like turning a microphone down for a nearby shout, then up for a faraway voice. STC acts on the receiver, never on the transmitter, and it does not change bearing resolution, how well the radar separates targets side by side.

params.title: STC turned up
labels: STC turned up: the clutter fades
Sea return decreases around the center of the PPI
The distant echo still shows at full strength

onScreen: Sea return decreases on the PPI
scenes.narration: Here's the result on the screen. With STC turned up, the clutter around the center fades. So the STC circuit is used to decrease sea return on a radar receiver, reducing the sea clutter around the center of the PPI scope. On the exam, watch for trap answers that say STC increases sensitivity for close targets, increases stability or selectivity, improves bearing resolution, or increases sea return. It does none of those. It decreases sensitivity only for close objects, so that distant echo near the edge still shows at full strength.

params.title: Setting and troubleshooting STC
items: The operator sets it with the front-panel sea clutter control
The STC circuit controls the suppression of sea clutter
Sea clutter won't reduce with the front-panel controls? Suspect a faulty STC circuit
FTC, fast time constant, is the rain clutter control, not sea return

onScreen: Can't reduce sea clutter: faulty STC circuit
scenes.narration: Who sets the STC? The operator, with the front-panel sea clutter control. The STC circuit is what controls the suppression of sea clutter. The exam's wrong choices are the EBL circuit, which draws the electronic bearing line, the local oscillator and the audio amplifier. So here's a troubleshooting question. If sea clutter cannot be effectively reduced with the front panel controls, which circuit do you suspect? A faulty STC circuit. Don't be tempted by FTC, the fast time constant circuit. FTC is the rain clutter control: it trims the long smear that rain makes, and it has nothing to do with sea return.

params.title: The most common interference
items: Weather: echoes from rain and snow
Sea return: echoes from nearby waves
Countered by the FTC rain control and the STC sea control

onScreen: FTC rain control, STC sea control
scenes.narration: Step back for a moment. Rain and waves are the 2 big troublemakers. In a radar receiver, the most common types of interference are weather and sea return: echoes from rain or snow, and echoes from the waves near the ship. The exam's wrong choices pair them with thermal noise, electrical interference or jamming, which is deliberate interference. Those exist, but they aren't the most common. Weather and sea return are countered by the FTC rain control and the STC sea control. Thermal noise does deserve its own look, though, because it sets the limit on how weak an echo the receiver can ever detect.

params.title: Where receiver noise comes from
items: Noise: random electrical jitter, heard as hiss and seen as speckle
Thermal noise: electrons jiggling with heat in every component
Primary cause: thermal noise from the receiver's own components
Worst in the mixer and the first IF stages

onScreen: Thermal noise: electrons jiggling with heat
Primary cause: the receiver's own components
scenes.narration: We met noise back in the IF amplifier: random electrical jitter, like the hiss you hear between stations on a radio. Where does it come from in a radar receiver? Mostly from the receiver itself. Inside every component, such as a resistor, a part that limits current, the electrons are constantly jiggling with heat. That random motion makes tiny random voltages, called thermal noise. So the primary cause of noise in a radar receiver is thermal noise caused by the receiver's own components, especially the mixer and the first IF stages. Why those? That's where the echo is weakest, and any noise added there gets amplified by every stage after it. Electrical causes, atmospheric changes and poor grounding are the exam's wrong choices.

params.title: Isolation keeps noise out
items: Shielding: metal enclosures around sensitive circuits
Physical separation from noisy equipment
Decoupling of power and signal leads
Keeps noise from the modulator, transmitter and other equipment out

onScreen: Isolation: one of the best ways to reduce noise
Decoupling of power and signal leads
scenes.narration: Thermal noise is built in, but noise from outside can be kept out. One of the best methods of reducing noise in a radar receiver is isolation. That means 3 things. Shielding: metal enclosures around sensitive circuits, so outside noise can't reach them. Physical separation: keeping the receiver away from noisy equipment. And decoupling of power and signal leads, the wires that carry power and signals in: small filters on those wires block noise from riding in along them. Together they keep noise from the modulator, the transmitter and other equipment out of the receiver. The wrong choices, changing the frequency, replacing the resonant cavity or changing the IF strip, don't remove the source of the noise.

params.title: What noise does to the picture
labels: Noise shows as erratic video and sharp changes in intensity
Not as fixed black spots or changes in bearings
A small target's weak echo is masked by the noise
A large target's strong echo stands well above it

onScreen: Not black spots or bearing changes
scenes.narration: What does noise look like on the screen? Modern radars use an LCD, a liquid crystal display, like a flat computer screen. Noise can appear on it as erratic video and sharp changes in intensity, meaning brightness: a restless speckle that flickers from moment to moment, because noise is random. It does not show up as fixed black spots, or as changes in bearings. And what can noise do to targets? It can mask small targets. Their weak echoes are no stronger than the noise, so they get lost in it. Large targets return strong echoes that stand well above the noise, so they stay clear. Noise masks small targets, not larger ones.

params.title: Radar heard on a communications receiver
labels: Radar pulses repeat at a fixed pulse repetition frequency (PRF)
Heard on a communications receiver as a steady tone
Unlike random static or hiss

scenes.narration: Radar can also interfere with other equipment. What does radar interference sound like on a nearby communications receiver? A steady tone. Here's why. A radar transmits its pulses at a fixed pulse repetition frequency, or PRF, the number of pulses it sends each second, typically hundreds or thousands. A receiver that picks them up hears a click for every pulse, and clicks repeating that fast, at a constant rate, blend into a tone of steady pitch. That's quite unlike static or hiss, which are random, and unlike a varying tone, because the PRF doesn't change.

params.title: MTI: moving target indication
items: MTI: a filter that blocks out stationary targets, allowing only moving targets to be detected
It compares each echo with the one from the pulse before
Fixed objects and ground clutter return the same echo: they cancel
A moving target's echo changes through Doppler shift: it remains

onScreen: Compares each echo with the one before
Moving targets change by Doppler shift
scenes.narration: Back to the radar's own picture. One more way to clean it up is MTI, moving target indication. The MTI circuit is a filter, a circuit that passes some signals and blocks others. This one blocks out stationary targets, allowing only moving targets to be detected. How can it tell? It compares each echo with the echo from the pulse before. Land, buildings and other fixed objects, along with ground clutter, return the same echo every time, so they cancel out. A moving target's echo changes from pulse to pulse through Doppler shift, a change in frequency caused by motion, like a siren's pitch dropping as an ambulance passes. So it survives.

params.title: MTI switched on
labels: MTI on: land and fixed clutter vanish
Ships under way remain
Only moving targets are displayed

scenes.narration: Here's the result on the screen. Switch MTI on, and the coastline, moored buoys and ground clutter vanish, while ships under way remain. Watch the traps. Receiver gain that increases with time is STC, not MTI. MTI doesn't act as a mixer or monitor transmitter interference, and it won't pick up targets that aren't moving. So when the receiver employs an MTI circuit, only moving targets will be displayed.

params.title: Glint: a faulty MTI filter
items: MTI cancels fixed clutter identically from pulse to pulse
A faulty MTI filter no longer cancels it identically
The clutter shifts with each pulse: that's glint
Not a memory failure, low AFC voltage or electrical interference

onScreen: MTI cancels clutter identically each pulse
Faulty MTI filter: it no longer does
Not memory, AFC or electrical interference
scenes.narration: What happens when the MTI filter goes wrong? Its whole trick is cancelling fixed clutter in exactly the same way from one pulse to the next. If the MTI filter is functioning improperly, it no longer cancels the clutter identically, so leftover bits of clutter shift around with each radar pulse. That condition is called glint. So if the exam asks what can cause glint, a shifting of clutter with each radar pulse, the answer is an improperly functioning MTI filter. Not a memory failure, low AFC voltage, or interference from electrical equipment.

params.title: Analog or digital receiver
rows: Passes the varying signal level along

scenes.narration: MTI works by comparing echoes, and many modern radars do that kind of processing digitally. That brings us to an exam question: what's the main difference between an analog and a digital receiver? An analog receiver simply passes the signal level along as it varies, smoothly, like a dimmer switch. A digital receiver adds decision circuitry. It compares the signal against a threshold, a set dividing line, and declares each moment either on or off, a 1 or a 0, like a light switch. So the main difference is the presence of decision circuitry to distinguish between on and off signal levels. The wrong choices, special amplification, no need for AGC, or no distortion, don't define the difference.

callouts.label: A comparator: an amplifier comparing its 2 inputs
Output: nominally high at 4.5 volts, low at −4.5 volts
The input signal goes to the inverting (−) input
2 resistors feed part of the output back to the + input

onScreen: Resistors feed back to the + input
scenes.narration: The simplest decision circuit is a comparator, and the exam shows one in Figure 8C11. The triangle is an amplifier with 2 inputs, marked minus and plus, and enormous gain. It compares them: if the plus input is higher, the output swings all the way high; if the minus input is higher, it swings all the way low. Here the output's nominal, or intended, high is 4.5 volts, and its low is minus 4.5 volts. The input signal goes to the minus input, called the inverting input, because when the input goes up, the output goes down. The plus input is the noninverting input. On the right, 2 resistors feed part of the output back to the noninverting input.

params.title: Figure 8C11: the resistors form a divider

callouts.label: 5K and 2K: 5 kilohms and 2 kilohms (1 kilohm = 1000 ohms)
In series from the output to ground, they share the output voltage
The + input, at their junction, gets the 2 kΩ resistor's share
That share is the threshold the input must cross

onScreen: A divider from the output to ground
The + input gets the 2 kΩ share
scenes.narration: So what do those resistors do? They're marked 5K and 2K, meaning 5 kilohms and 2 kilohms. Resistance, how strongly a part limits current, is measured in ohms, and a kilohm is 1000 ohms. The 2 resistors sit in series between the output and ground, the circuit's 0 volt reference. That makes them a divider: the output voltage is shared between them in proportion to their size. The plus input connects at their junction, so it gets the 2 kilohm resistor's share. That share is the threshold, the level the input must cross to flip the output.

params.title: A Schmitt trigger has 2 trip points
items: The threshold moves with the output
Output high, +4.5 V: the upper trip point; the input must rise above it
Output low, −4.5 V: the lower trip point; the input must fall below it
2 trip points stop chatter: an inverting Schmitt trigger comparator

onScreen: The threshold moves with the output
scenes.narration: But the output itself changes, so the threshold moves with it. While the output is high, plus 4.5 volts, the threshold is positive: the upper trip point. The input must rise above it to flip the output low. Once the output is low, minus 4.5 volts, the threshold is negative: the lower trip point. Now the input must fall below that to flip it back. Why bother with 2? With a single threshold, a noisy input hovering near it would make the output chatter back and forth. 2 trip points stop that, like a thermostat that switches on at one temperature and off at another. This circuit is an inverting Schmitt trigger comparator.

Now the numbers. V sub trip is the trip point voltage. The fraction fed back is the 2 kilohm resistor's share: 2 kilohms over the total, 5 kilohms plus 2 kilohms. Multiply that by the output voltage, plus or minus 4.5 volts. Step 1: 5 plus 2 is 7, so the fraction is 2 over 7. Step 2: 4.5 times 2 over 7 is about 1.2857 volts, which the exam shortens to 1.285. So the upper trip point is plus 1.285 volts, and the lower is minus 1.285 volts. Does it make sense? 2 over 7 is a bit more than a quarter, and 1.285 is a bit more than a quarter of 4.5. That rules out traps like 4.5 and 0 volts, or 2.5 and 2 volts.

params.title: Sine in: when the output goes high
labels: Halfway through each cycle, at 180°, the input falls through zero
Just past that, it crosses the lower trip point, −1.285 V
The output's leading edge: 180° after the positive zero crossing
Not 45° after a zero crossing or a peak

onScreen: It crosses the lower trip point
Leading edge 180° after the positive zero crossing
scenes.narration: Next, feed a sine wave, a smooth up-and-down signal, into Figure 8C11. Points along one cycle, one complete up and down, are counted in degrees, like positions around a circle. The wave crosses zero going up at the start, called the positive zero crossing, and halfway through the cycle, at 180 degrees, it crosses zero going down. When does the output's leading edge, its jump to high, come? Remember, the comparator inverts, so the output goes high only when the falling input passes the lower trip point, minus 1.285 volts, just past that downward zero crossing. That's why the leading edge of the output waveform occurs 180 degrees after the positive zero crossing of the input. It does not trail a zero crossing or a peak by 45 degrees.

params.title: How a switching power supply works
items: A power supply turns the ship's AC into steady DC
A switching supply: a transistor switches the DC on and off very fast
A filter smooths the switched pulses into steady DC
The longer the switch stays on, the higher the output

onScreen: Power supply: AC in, steady DC out
A transistor switches on and off very fast
scenes.narration: That's the comparator. Circuits like it also work inside power supplies, the last part of the receiver we'll cover. Every circuit we've met runs on steady DC, and the power supply makes it from the ship's AC, alternating current, which flows back and forth. A modern radar uses a switching power supply. It first rectifies the AC into rough DC. Then a transistor, acting as a fast electronic switch, turns that DC on and off many thousands of times a second. Finally, a filter smooths the pulses into steady DC. Picture a tap flicked on and off very fast: the longer it stays open each time, the more water flows on average. The switch works the same way.

params.title: Duty cycle sets the output
labels: Period T: one complete on-off cycle, T = 1 ÷ switching frequency
Duty cycle = ON time ÷ period
V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>in</sub> × duty cycle

scenes.narration: So how long is the switch on, and what does that do to the output? Each complete on-off cycle takes a fixed time called the period, T. The period is 1 over the switching frequency, the number of on-off cycles each second. The fraction of each period that the switch spends on is called the duty cycle: the ON time divided by the period. A switching regulator, the circuit that holds a supply's output steady, often switches at a constant frequency and varies only the ON time. In a constant frequency switching regulator, the output voltage is the input voltage times the duty cycle. A switch that's on for half of every period gives half the input voltage; on for most of the period, most of it.

params.title: Switching regulator output voltage
params.answer: V<sub>out</sub> = 89.1 V DC; the 1 A load isn't used

scenes.narration: The exam's example: a constant frequency switching regulator has 165 volts DC in and switches at 20 kilohertz, 20 thousand times a second. Its ON time is 27 microseconds, millionths of a second, while it supplies 1 ampere of current to its load, the circuits it powers. What's the output voltage? Step 1, the period: T equals 1 over 20 kilohertz, so 1 second shared among 20 thousand cycles, 50 microseconds each. Step 2, the duty cycle: 27 over 50 is 0.54. Step 3: V sub out equals 0.54 times 165 volts, which is 89.1 volts DC. Sensible? The switch is on just over half the time, and 89.1 is just over half of 165. The 1 ampere doesn't enter the calculation, so don't answer that it can't be determined.

params.title: No isolation transformer: a hidden danger

blocks.label: Grounded oscilloscope
blocks.note: Its ground clip is at 0 volts

scenes.narration: Before you measure anything in a live switching supply, here's a safety point the exam tests. Ground, remember, is the 0 volt reference; on a ship, that's the metal hull and the earth wiring. Many switching supplies rectify the AC line, the ship's live power wiring, directly, with no line isolation transformer, a transformer that keeps the circuit separate from the line. Without one, the supply's circuit common, the point you'd normally treat as its 0 volt reference, can sit at line potential: it's connected to the live AC line. Now bring in an oscilloscope, an instrument that draws a voltage on a screen. Its ground clip is wired to ground through its power cord.

params.title: Before probing a switching supply
items: A grounded clip on a common at line potential shorts the line to ground
The fault current can destroy the supply
So know the supply's design before power-on measurements
Not the reason: finding the filter capacitors to discharge them

onScreen: Grounded clip on a live common: a short
scenes.narration: Clip that grounded lead onto a circuit common at line potential, and you short the live line straight to ground. A huge current flows, which can destroy the supply. So before making power-on measurements, be familiar with the supply: if it does not use a line isolation transformer, you may destroy it with grounded test equipment. Knowing where the filter capacitors are, so they can be discharged, is good practice, but it's not the reason the exam wants. And don't believe that ungrounded test equipment can never cause a failure, or that knowing the supply means you can skip the schematic.

params.title: The power MOSFET switch
items: Power MOSFET: the transistor that does the switching
The voltage on its gate turns it on and off
Gate threshold: roughly 2 to 4 V; fully on: about 10 V
So the gate changes by greater than 2 volts, low to high

onScreen: Gate voltage turns it on and off
Threshold 2 to 4 V, fully on about 10 V
Gate changes by greater than 2 volts
scenes.narration: Now the switch itself. In a modern radar's switching supply, it's usually a power MOSFET, a metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor. It's controlled by the voltage on its gate terminal: low means off, high means on. A MOSFET's gate threshold, where it just begins to conduct, is roughly 2 to 4 volts, and it needs about 10 volts to switch fully on with little resistance. So when you monitor the gate voltage of a power MOSFET, you'd expect it to change from low to high by greater than 2 volts. Swings of 1 to 2 volts, or a few hundred microvolts, wouldn't even reach the threshold.

callouts.label: Q1, a power MOSFET, switches T1 at the high switching rate
T1, a transformer, passes the pulses to its secondary windings
CR6 and CR7: diodes that rectify the pulses
L1 and C6: a filter that smooths them into steady DC

scenes.narration: Let's see that MOSFET at work in Figure 8C10, the output section of a switching supply. On the left, Q1, the power MOSFET, switches T1, a transformer, on and off at the high switching rate. The primary winding, the coil Q1 drives, passes the pulses through its magnetic field to the secondary windings on the right. In the upper output, CR6 and CR7 are diodes, which rectify the pulses so they flow one way only. Then L1, a coil, and C6, a capacitor, form a filter. The coil resists sudden changes in current and the capacitor holds the voltage steady, so together they smooth the pulses into steady DC for the 12 volt output.

params.title: Probing Figure 8C10
rows: Junction of CR6, CR7 and L1
Pulsating DC much higher than line frequency
After the L1 and C6 filter

onScreen: CR6, CR7 and L1 junction: pulsating DC much higher than line frequency
scenes.narration: Time for the exam's question. With an oscilloscope, you measure from the junction of CR6, CR7 and L1 to ground. What waveform do you see? That point is after the diodes but before the L1 and C6 filter. The pulses have been rectified into one direction, which makes them pulsating DC, but they haven't been smoothed yet. And they pulse at Q1's switching rate, far above the line frequency, the 50 or 60 cycles a second of the ship's AC power. So the answer is pulsating DC much higher than line frequency. Filtered DC is what you'd see after the filter, and the line-frequency answers forget that Q1 switches far faster than the AC line alternates.

params.title: Key facts: Receiving Systems
items: No RF amplifier: the crystal mixer and klystron make a 30 or 60 MHz IF
AFC: the discriminator compares magnetron and klystron, and corrects the repeller
Gain = 20 log(V<sub>out</sub> ÷ V<sub>in</sub>): 2 µV to 2 V is 120 dB; AGC 20 to 40 dB
STC cuts close-range gain for sea clutter; FTC is for rain; MTI shows only moving targets
Switching supply: 89.1 V DC; Figure 8C11 trips at ±1.285 V

onScreen: No RF amplifier; IF of 30 or 60 MHz
scenes.narration: Let's wrap up with 5 things to remember. First, there's no RF amplifier: the crystal mixer and klystron local oscillator turn the echo into a 30 or 60 megahertz IF, where nearly all the gain happens. Second, AFC keeps the klystron one IF from the magnetron: the discriminator compares them and corrects the klystron's repeller voltage. Third, gain in decibels is 20 log of V sub out over V sub in, so 2 microvolts to 2 volts is 120 decibels, and AGC can vary it by 20 to 40 decibels. Fourth, STC tames sea clutter by cutting gain for close echoes, FTC handles rain, and MTI shows only moving targets. Fifth, the worked numbers: the switching regulator gives 89.1 volts, and Figure 8C11 trips at plus and minus 1.285 volts.
